name: Aaron Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Aaron. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm head grower at Greenmoor, a community farm with about three hundred families paying in for a weekly veg box. We've also got forty outdoor pigs, five hundred laying hens and a small rotation of oats and clover. A normal day is feeding round at seven, then the polytunnels, then packing boxes on Tuesdays and Fridays. I check the crop plan with an AI assistant over breakfast, every day, it's basically my second brain.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you ask it, exactly?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Things like, the leeks in bed six have rust, what's the least-bad fix that keeps our organic status. Or I'll paste in the weather for the week and ask it to reshuffle the planting plan. It's wrong maybe one time in ten, so I check it. But it saves me an hour a day, easy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, honestly. I'd post something like, turns out the future is still mostly me on my knees in a polytunnel. People would find that funny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it changes very little for me. I'd keep using the tools I already use. The bit I was hoping for, cheap robots that small farms could share, just wouldn't come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going with the plan and keep using the assistant for the crop plan and the member emails. I'd still try the open-source weeding robot a group of growers is building, even if it's clunky. Mostly it's the same year as this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What were you hoping a robot would take off your hands?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Weeding the carrots by hand. Eight of us lying on a bed on a board, inching along. Every June I lie face down on a plank for a week, and every June I think a robot should be doing this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does a flat picture like this cost you anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay, a little. Food prices stay where they are, the big farms stay cheaper than us, and we keep scraping by on members' goodwill. AI wasn't going to fix that on its own anyway.

S0.say: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed and that the future is apparently still me on my knees in a polytunnel. I'd post it as a joke and people would find it funny.
S0.think: I think it changes very little for me, since I already use the tools that would exist. The thing I hoped for, cheap robots small farms could share, just wouldn't come.
S0.do: Keeps using the AI assistant for crop planning and member emails and carries on with the farm plan. Still tries the clunky open-source weeding robot that a group of growers is building.
S0.feel: Calm but a little flat, as if a promise fell through.
S0.quote: Every June I lie face down on a plank for a week, and every June I think a robot should be doing this.
S0.fieldNote: Aaron is the rare farmer who would be let down if AI fizzled. He already uses it every day and wants robots for the backbreaking jobs, like hand-weeding carrots. His real money worry is cheap food from big farms, which AI wouldn't change in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is our chance, but only if the machines are shared and not just bought by the biggest estates. I'd be pushing hard for small farms to club together. I'd post about it constantly, my friends would get sick of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do well out of it, I think. I already know the tools and I'm the kind of person who signs up for the trial. The risk is that I'm the only one at Greenmoor who's excited and the volunteers feel pushed out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up a machinery-sharing group with three or four nearby growers in the first six months, to buy one weeding robot between us. Maybe twelve thousand each, with a grant if we can get one. I'd keep learning the newest planning tools and train the others on our team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Greenmoor would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The volunteers, mostly retired folks who come on Wednesdays. Some of them come for the company more than the work. I'd make sure there's still something for them to do with their hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're excited, but you're also describing people losing what they come for. How do you square that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You're right, and I do worry about it. If the robot weeds the carrots and the volunteers stop coming, we've saved time and lost the farm's whole reason to exist. So I'd keep the hand jobs that people actually like.

S1.say: I'd say this is our chance, but only if the machines are shared and not just bought by the biggest estates. I'd be pushing small farms to club together and posting about it constantly.
S1.think: I think I'd do well, because I already know the tools and sign up for trials. The risk is being the only excited one and leaving the volunteers feeling pushed out.
S1.do: Sets up a machinery-sharing group with three or four nearby growers in the first six months to buy one weeding robot, at around twelve thousand each with a grant if possible. Keeps learning new planning tools and trains his team.
S1.feel: Calm and openly excited, with a small worry about the volunteers.
S1.quote: If the robot weeds the carrots and the volunteers stop coming, we've saved time and lost the farm's whole reason to exist.
S1.fieldNote: Aaron's progressive views and love of technology meet in the idea of shared machines. When challenged, he saw on his own that saving time could cost the farm its community. He plans to keep the hand jobs people enjoy, which shows he's thinking beyond efficiency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast and the public has to own a share of it. If robots do all the work, everyone should get a cut. I'd be online every night arguing for that, and at the council.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's not the robots on our farm that scare me, I'd love them. It's that big farms get them first, food gets even cheaper, and three hundred families stop paying extra for our boxes. And Jonah writes software, so his job would be gone even faster than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get our sharing group to buy the robots now, before prices spike, even if it means a loan. I'd stop spending on anything fun and put away what I can, because we've only got about three months. And I'd join every campaign for a robot dividend, a payment to everyone from what the machines earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited and scared at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years of warning do to your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I can't build anything slowly. I'd have to take risks I'd normally think about for a season, like borrowing for kit before I know it works. That's not how you do farming, you test a bed first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the conversation with Jonah be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonah would be the one panicking, and I'd be the one saying it'll be fine. I'm the farmer telling the software developer not to worry about robots, which is a sentence I never thought I'd say.

S2.say: I'd say this is too fast and the public has to own a share of it, so everyone gets a cut if robots do the work. I'd argue that online every night and at the council.
S2.think: I think the robots on our farm would be welcome, but cheap food from big farms could drain our members, and my partner Jonah's software job would go even faster than mine. Three months of savings doesn't go far.
S2.do: Gets the machinery group to buy robots early, even with a loan, before prices rise. Cuts fun spending to save more and joins campaigns for a robot dividend paid to everyone.
S2.feel: Anxious, with excitement and fear mixed together.
S2.quote: I'm the farmer telling the software developer not to worry about robots, which is a sentence I never thought I'd say.
S2.fieldNote: Even in the fast picture Aaron welcomes the machines on his own farm; his fear is the market and his partner's job. Two years would force him to take risks he would normally test first. The role reversal with his software developer partner amused and unsettled him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to set up co-ops so farmers own the robots instead of renting them. That's my whole pitch. I'd be talking to the growers' network about it every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years suits me, really. I can test the kit properly, and Greenmoor could become the farm people visit to see how it's done. The members might stay if we're the local farm that's also the clever one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd test two robots on our beds in the first year, a weeder and a hen-house cleaner. I'd put some of my own savings into the sharing co-op as a member share, maybe two thousand. And I'd get Jonah to help write a simple guide for other small farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is five years different from the two-year picture for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can do this like a farmer and not like a gambler. Two years, I'm buying blind. Five years, I trial it, I watch what breaks, I tell the neighbours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think you're doing in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd be teaching other farms, or running the robot co-op. I honestly don't know if anyone needs a head grower when the machines can grow. Best case, I'm the guy who taught the robots where the slugs hide.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to set up co-ops so farmers own the robots instead of renting them. I'd make that pitch to the growers' network every month.
S3.think: I think five years suits me because I can test the kit properly and Greenmoor could become a model farm. The members might stay if we're known as the clever local farm.
S3.do: Tests a weeding robot and a hen-house cleaning robot in the first year and puts about two thousand of his savings into the sharing co-op. Writes a simple guide for other small farms with his partner.
S3.quote: Best case, I'm the guy who taught the robots where the slugs hide.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Aaron farms the change like a crop: trial, watch, share. He sees a role as the local teacher of the new methods. His joke about teaching robots where slugs hide hides a real doubt about whether a head grower will be needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this could be the best thing to happen to small farming in a century, if we share it properly. A decade is long enough to get the rules right. I'd be one of the people writing to the papers about it, in a good way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it feels good. I'd be 37, I'd have ten years of learning the machines, and I'd probably be ahead of most people. The worry is everyone else, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep automating step by step, one job per season. I'd start offering workshops to other farms for a fee, maybe weekends. And I'd put a bit into the co-op every year so we own the kit outright by the time it all lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone in your life this picture worries you about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad, actually. He was a dairy worker, lost his job when the farm he worked on sold to a big outfit. He's 62 now. If this comes, I'd want him to get something out of it, not just watch again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If machines do most of the work by 2036, would you want to still be farming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want that, yes. I don't want to be the last farmer; I want to be the first one who gets Fridays off. That's the whole dream really.

S4.say: I'd say this could be the best thing for small farming in a century if we share it properly, and a decade is long enough to get the rules right. I'd write to the papers making that case.
S4.think: I think at 37, with ten years of learning the machines, I'd be ahead of most people. My worry is for everyone else, not for me.
S4.do: Automates one job per season, starts paid weekend workshops for other farms and puts a little into the co-op every year so it owns its machines outright by 2036.
S4.feel: Calm and hopeful, with worry kept for others like his father.
S4.quote: I don't want to be the last farmer; I want to be the first one who gets Fridays off.
S4.fieldNote: The long runway suits Aaron's style perfectly and he becomes almost optimistic. His father's past job loss to a farm takeover shapes his insistence on sharing the gains. His dream is less work, not no work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not because of the robots, but because there'd be no time to set up the co-ops, so the big estates would own everything. What would help is grants or cheap loans for groups of small farms to buy machines together, and some kind of payment for everyone out of what the machines earn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who owns the robots. Everybody asks if the robot takes your job. Nobody asks whose name is on the robot's paperwork, and that's the only question that matters.

headlineQuote: Nobody asks whose name is on the robot's paperwork, and that's the only question that matters.
portrait: Aaron Evans, 27, is head grower at Greenmoor, a community farm with veg boxes, pigs and hens, and he uses an AI assistant every day. He'd be slightly disappointed if AI fizzled and openly excited by steady change, as long as small farms can share the machines. The two-year picture makes him anxious, not because of robots on his farm but because big estates would win and his partner Jonah's software job would go. With five or ten years he plans to trial machines, run a co-op and teach other farms, and he becomes calm and even hopeful.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there would be no time for small farms to form co-ops and big estates would end up owning the machines.
whatWouldHelp: Grants or cheap loans for groups of small farms to buy machines together, and a payment to everyone from what the machines earn.
